Well Site Relocation Agreement fully executed 6.7.22

description:
The City of Flagler Beach and JTL Grand Landings Holdings, LLC executed the Well Site Relocation Agreement on June 2, 2022. Under Section 4 of the Agreement, the City is responsible for the cost of all materials and electrical improvements required to support the relocation of City water infrastructure. This includes electrical improvements and demolitions necessary to energize new or revised well sites.
To provide electrical service to a City well located within the Enclave at Seminole Palms, Florida Power & Light (FPL) required relocation and scrapping of an existing power pole. CRE‑KL Seminole Woods Owner, LLC (successor to the Developer for this area) paid FPL directly and submitted Invoice #1 (January 30, 2025) in the amount of $118,019.00 for “Power Pole Relocation/Scrapping.”
This work was required to energize the City’s well and is therefore a reimbursable City Cost under the Agreement.
Staff has reviewed the documentation and confirmed that the work directly supports City water infrastructure and is contractually reimbursable.
1. What This Action AccomplishesThis action fulfills the City’s contractual obligation under the Well Site Relocation Agreement by reimbursing the Developer (CRE‑KL Seminole Woods Owner, LLC) for the cost of relocating an FPL power pole that was required to energize a City well. Without this relocation, the well cannot receive electrical service and therefore cannot operate.
2. Why We Are Doing This (Regulatory, Contractual, and Operational Justification)
A. Contractual RequirementThe Well Site Relocation Agreement (June 2, 2022) explicitly states that the City must pay for:
“any and all materials required to complete the City Improvements,” including
“electrical improvements and all electrical demolitions necessary for the relocation of the City’s Water Main,” and that the City must reimburse the Developer for these costs “as authenticated by receipts.”
The FPL relocation is an electrical improvement required to energize a City well. Therefore, the City is legally obligated to reimburse the cost.
B. Operational NecessityThe relocated power pole provides electrical service to a City well that supplies raw water to the City’s potable water system. Without electrical service:
the well cannot pump water,
the City loses production capacity,
redundancy and resiliency are reduced,
and regulatory compliance risks increase.
C. Developer Paid the Cost UpfrontFPL requires payment before performing relocation work. The Developer paid the FPL invoice and submitted the required documentation to the City. The City must now reimburse the Developer per the Agreement.
3. Deliverables (What the City Receives / What This Payment Covers)
A. Completed FPL Power Pole RelocationThe relocation and scrapping of an existing FPL power pole to allow electrical service to reach the City well. This includes:
removal of the old pole,
installation of the new pole,
reconnection of electrical infrastructure,
service alignment to the City’s well site.
B. Energized Electrical Service to the City WellThe well now has the electrical capacity required for:
pump operation,
telemetry and controls,
SCADA integration,
safety and monitoring systems.
C. Compliance with the Well Site Relocation AgreementThis payment satisfies the City’s obligation under Section 4 (“City’s Costs”). It prevents:
breach of contract,
potential legal exposure,
delays in well activation.
4. Measured Outcomes (How We Know This Was Successful)
Outcome 1 — Well is Fully EnergizedElectrical service is active and stable at the well site.
Outcome 2 — Water Production Capacity is MaintainedThe well can now operate as part of the City’s raw water supply system.
Outcome 3 — Contractual Compliance AchievedThe City meets its obligations under the Agreement, avoiding disputes or penalties.
Outcome 4 — Infrastructure Resiliency ImprovedThe relocated well and associated electrical service support long‑term system reliability.
title: Resolution 2026‑41. A Resolution by the City Commission of the City of Flagler Beach approving reimbursement to CRE‑KL Seminole Woods Owner, LLC for FPL power‑pole relocation required to provide electrical service to a City well; providing for conflict and an effective date.

description:
Submitted by Commissioner J. Cunningham:
The City Manager serves at the direction of the City Commission and is responsible for the administration and day-to-day operations of the City. As the chief executive officer of the City, the City Manager is entrusted with implementing Commission policy, overseeing municipal operations, managing public resources, and advancing the strategic priorities established by the elected governing body.
Automatic renewal provisions in executive employment agreements can weaken direct oversight and reduce meaningful accountability by allowing a contract to continue without deliberate annual review by the City Commission. The Commission has a fiduciary responsibility to regularly evaluate leadership effectiveness, fiscal management, responsiveness to Commission direction, operational performance, and progress toward City goals and priorities.
Requiring an annual review of the City Manager’s employment agreement in conjunction with a formal performance evaluation ensures that the Commission affirmatively determines whether the terms of the agreement remain appropriate based on the City’s current financial conditions, operational needs, strategic objectives, and community expectations.
An annual review process also establishes a transparent and structured framework for:
• Establishing measurable goals and expectations
• Evaluating leadership performance and organizational effectiveness
• Addressing areas of concern or improvement
• Reviewing compensation and contract terms based upon documented performance
• Ensuring continued alignment between the Commission and executive administration
DISCUSSION:
Most municipalities do not utilize automatic renewal provisions in City Manager employment agreements because the City Manager serves directly at the pleasure of the elected governing body. Municipal governance best practices generally favor active oversight and affirmative annual review rather than passive contract continuation.
Automatic renewals can undermine one of the City Commission’s most important responsibilities: regularly evaluating executive leadership and making deliberate decisions regarding continued employment, compensation, contract terms, and organizational performance.
Municipalities commonly avoid automatic renewal clauses for several reasons:
1. They preserve direct accountability to elected officials and the public.
2. They require affirmative public action by the governing body rather than allowing contracts to extend automatically without discussion.
3. They ensure annual performance evaluations occur in a timely and meaningful manner.
4. They provide flexibility for changing financial conditions, policy priorities, operational needs, and community expectations.
5. They reduce the risk of “evergreen” contracts that continuously extend and may increase severance obligations or create unnecessary legal complications.
6. They reinforce transparency by requiring employment discussions and renewal decisions to occur publicly.
7. They strengthen the Commission’s oversight authority and governance role.
In many municipalities, City Manager contracts are intentionally structured with fixed terms requiring periodic review and affirmative renewal because the relationship between the governing body and the City Manager is fundamentally based upon confidence, trust, responsiveness, accountability, and performance.
Professional municipal governance organizations, including the International City/County Management Association, emphasize the importance of regular performance evaluations, measurable goal setting, accountability standards, and ongoing executive oversight as recognized best practices in local government management. Removing automatic renewal language does not prohibit future renewals or long-term employment stability. A properly structured annual evaluation process still allows the City Commission to renew, extend, or amend the agreement when performance is satisfactory and continued leadership is in the best interest of the City. The key distinction is that continuation of the agreement occurs through deliberate public action following review and evaluation rather than through automatic extension without formal Commission consideration.
title: Resolution 2026-43. A Resolution of the City Commission of the City of Flagler Beach, Florida, amending the Employment Agreement of the City Manager to remove any automatic renewal provision; requiring an annual performance evaluation and annual review of the Employment Agreement by the City Commission; providing for implementation; and providing for an effective date.
Public Hearings

The City intends to distribute a package soliciting bids for Janitorial Services in early 2027, so we are set with coverage of service at the end of the contract in April 2027.

description:
Three of the Seats are at term. Four applications were received. Please score the applicants with 1 being your best candidate. The three persons receiving the lowest scores will be selected to a three-year term.
Although not necessary, it may be worth considering "standardizing" the terms and appointments of official City boards and commissions (such as the Planning and Architectural Review Board). The City Code requires that the seven members of the Planning and Architectural Review Board be residents of the City and serve three-year terms, with no more than three terms expiring in one year. As can be observed, current terms on the Planning and Architectural Review Board expire in February and May.
I suggest that the pending three appointments to the Planning and Architectural Review Board expire on December 31, 2029. The term scheduled to expire in May, 2027, as well as one of the terms scheduled to expire in February, 2028, should both be appointed for terms to expire on December 31, 2030. The final two terms scheduled to expire in February, 2028 should both be appointed for terms to expire on December 31, 2031. If accepted, the City Commission would consider appointments each year at the December City Commission Regular Meeting for terms to begin on January 1.

description:
Approximately two years ago, the City Commission endorsed an application to the Flagler County Tourist Development Council (TDC) to seek funding support for a Pier enhancement project designated as the Beachwalk Project. As conceived, the Beachwalk was composed of three phases: Phase I- reconfiguration of the A-frame facilities (restrooms, radio station, former bait shop); Phase II- construction of the Promenade, a 4,000 square foot open-air deck immediately south of the Pier's A-frame facilities; Phase III- re-construction of the oceanfront boardwalk from approximately S. 3rd Street to S. 7th Street. The City was awarded approximately $750,000 from the TDC for the project which was to be matched with a similar $750,000 contribution from the City (the grant was specifically related to Phases I and II. The estimated cost for each phase was approximately $1,300,000.
After preliminary review, the Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) has indicated that the Beachwalk Phases I and II will require additional dune construction- the profile of the required dune is to match the dunes constructed by the United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) in 2024. The federal project for that effort only went as far north as S. 6th Street; the Flagler County effort associated with the USACE effort was constructed to a lesser profile from S. 6th Street to N. 7th Street. An estimate provided by Mr. Gabriel Perdomo (Moffatt & Nichol, the Beachwalk Project design engineer) was that the additional dune construction would cost $300,000. Given the additional dune construction requirement and the related delay, the City Commission subsequently withdrew the Beachwalk Project from TDC consideration, returning the $750,000 award (the award was for a reimbursement, so no funds had been transferred). As a result, the Beachwalk Project, as originally conceived, was suspended.
In light of the aforementioned circumstances, the City Commission is presented an opportunity to re-visit the Beachwalk Project with a proposal from Mr. Perdomo to proceed with the survey, design, and permitting for the necessary dune construction. Consider the following:Mr. Edgar Fernandez has been working with State officials to re-purpose a portion of the State funds provided for the Pier Reconstruction Project to support the Beachwalk Project. The State has allocated $4,500,000 for the City's required 12.5% contribution for the Pier Project. Using a conservative final construction cost estimate of $16,000,000, the City's contribution would be $2,000,000, significantly less than the $4,500,000 provided. The State funds, though, if not utilized for the Pier Project, are required to be returned to the State (a loss of $2,500,000 to the City). Mr. Fernandez' efforts have been with State legislators and State departmental officials to re-allocate the $2,500,000 for the Pier-related Beachwalk Project. A key consideration for that request is that the original State appropriation was based upon the role of the Pier related to "tourism" and that the Beachwalk Project would further support the tourist economy in Flagler Beach. With the possibility of securing the $2,500,000 State funding combined with the $750,000 currently budgeted for the Beachwalk Project, the City would have $3,250,000 available for the Beachwalk Project. That funding would be sufficient for the survey/design/permitting ($180,000), the dune construction ($300,000), and Phases I and II of the Beachwalk ($2,700,000): total current estimate, $3,180,000, leaving a small margin of revenues ($70,000).
DEP officials have directed the City to pursue dune reconstruction grants (a 50%/50% program) for additional funding to reduce the estimated $300,000 dune cost.
Phase III of the Beachwalk Project (the boardwalk) has been proposed to be included as part of the FDOT SUN Trail effort currently under review and as part of the City's recent application to the Volusia-Flagler Transportation Planning Organization.
Given those conditions, the City Commission is requested to consider the proposal from Moffatt & Nichol for survey, design, and permitting for the required dune construction to support the Beachwalk Project.

attachments.name: 2026-32 S. Central Ave Water Main Design Services
South Central WM Replacement Ph. 2 Scope of Services Revised

description:
The existing water main along South Central Avenue is composed of asbestos cement (AC) pipe installed several decades ago. AC pipe is no longer manufactured, is considered obsolete, and becomes increasingly brittle with age. As the pipe deteriorates, the risk of breaks, leaks, and service interruptions increases significantly. Emergency repairs are costly, disruptive to residents, and often require temporary road closures.
Replacing this pipe is not optional—it is a necessary investment in the City’s core infrastructure. The project also supports long-term system resiliency by upgrading pipe size from eight inches to ten inches, improving flow capacity and pressure reliability. Additionally, installing a reclaimed water main ("dryline") now avoids future excavation and reduces long-term construction impacts.
Phase 1 of the S. Central Avenue Water Main Project provided valuable insight into the condition of the existing infrastructure and the complexity of construction along South Central Avenue. Several key findings influenced the approach to Phase 2:Location of Existing Pipe: South of S. 9th Street, the existing water main was found to be outside the roadway pavement, reducing anticipated restoration costs.
Updated Unit Costs: Actual construction costs from Phase 1 were used to refine the cost estimate for Phase 2, resulting in a more accurate and defensible budget.
Phased Construction Approach: To better align with annual funding availability and minimize disruption to residents, Phase 2 will be constructed in smaller segments over multiple years.
Coordination with Other Utilities: Phase 1 revealed several utility conflicts that required additional coordination. Phase 2 incorporates a more robust utility coordination process to reduce delays.
These adjustments reflect responsible project management and ensure that Phase 2 is delivered efficiently and cost‑effectively.
What This Project Does:
Replaces approximately 7,000 linear feet of obsolete 8‑inch AC water main with 10‑inch PVC.
Installs 7,000 linear feet of 8‑inch reclaimed water main (“dryline”).
Continues the City’s multi‑year beachside water system renewal program.
Provides design, permitting, and bidding documents for the first constructed portion (S. 3rd to S. 6th).
Directly supports the City’s goals of maintaining reliable utility service, reducing maintenance costs, and preparing for future reclaimed water expansion.
Why It Matters:
AC pipe is outdated, brittle, and prone to failure
Phase 1 is complete; Phase 2 continues the system upgrade
Reduces maintenance costs and improves reliability
Supports long‑term capital planning and regulatory compliance
Outcome: Approval allows design and permitting to begin immediately.
Mead & Hunt, Inc. submitted a revised Scope of Services dated March 6, 2026, covering project management, data collection, design development (60%, 90%, and 100%), permitting assistance, and bidding assistance for the first constructed portion (South 3rd Street to South 6th Street). Construction phase services will be provided under a future proposal.
The City receives professional services that prepare the project for construction. These include:
Survey & Data Collection
Full topographic and boundary survey of the project corridor.
Identification of existing utilities, including water, wastewater, stormwater, and private utilities.
Field verification of conditions, including pavement, driveways, and drainage features.
Photographic documentation for design and future reference.
Design Documents
60% Design: Preliminary layout, pipe alignment, utility conflicts, and initial cost estimate.
90% Design: Refined plans, specifications, and updated cost estimate suitable for permitting.
100% Design: Final bid‑ready plans and specifications.
Permitting
Preparation and submittal of the FDEP Specific Permit to Construct Public Water System Components.
Response to one Request for Additional Information (RAI).
Bidding Assistance
Preparation of draft and final bid documents.
Attendance at non-mandatory pre‑bid meeting.
Preparation of addenda.
Review of bids and recommendation of award.
These deliverables ensure the City receives a complete, permit‑ready, and bid‑ready project.
The City Commission’s approval of this resolution will authorize execution of the Task Order and allow design and permitting activities to begin. After design work and bidding has been completed/reviewed, the City Commission will be provided a Resolution to begin construction of Phase 2 of the S. Central Avenue Water Main Project.

attachments.name: Resolution Palm Harbor Feasibility Study Proposal

description:
The City continues to experience recurring nuisance flooding and limited drainage capacity within the Palm Harbor neighborhood. Previous stormwater studies have identified existing conditions and recommended improvements. However, the City seeks a more focused feasibility analysis to evaluate additional alternatives, refine drainage subbasins, and establish planning‑level costs for future capital improvements.
Freese and Nichols, Inc. (FNI), an engineering consultant under the City’s Continuing Services Agreement, submitted a proposal dated March 23, 2026, titled Palm Harbor Drainage Improvements Feasibility Study. The proposal includes:Project management and administration
Data collection, including review of previous studies, City records, LiDAR, and coordination of a design survey
A pre‑design field visit
Development of up to two conceptual drainage alternatives
Preliminary hydrologic analysis using the rational method
Coordination with the St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD) for a pre‑application meeting
Preparation of planning‑level cost estimates
Delivery of a Technical Memorandum summarizing findings, alternatives, costs, permitting considerations, and recommendations.
What This Project Will Accomplish
1. Give the City a clear picture of how Palm Harbor actually drainsThe study will map how water moves through the neighborhood using new survey data, LiDAR, and field checks. This replaces old assumptions with accurate information.
2. Identify realistic ways to reduce nuisance floodingThe consultant will create two improvement concepts, things like upgraded pipes, re‑graded swales, or hybrid systems, and show how each one would function.
3. Provide early cost ranges for each improvement optionThe City will know the approximate construction cost for each concept so it can plan future capital budgets.
4. Clarify what permits will be requiredThe consultant will meet with the Water Management District to understand what environmental permits will be needed and what constraints exist.
5. Give the City a defensible roadmap for next stepsThis study sets the stage for design, permitting, and construction. It does not build anything, it prepares the City to make informed decisions.
What the City Will Receive
1. Updated drainage basin mapsClear graphics showing 3–5 drainage subbasins and how water currently flows.
2. Two conceptual improvement alternativesEach alternative will include a simple planview layout, approximate pipe sizes or ditch sections, notes on constraints or conflicts.
3. Planning‑level construction cost estimates
Cost tables for each alternative, including contingencies.
4. A summary of permitting requirementsA written explanation of what the Water Management District will expect.
5. A full Technical Memorandum This will summarize existing conditions, alternatives, costs, permitting, and recommended next steps (Subsurface Utility Engineering, Geotechnical Investigation, etc.)
6. Supporting documentation
Kickoff meeting notes
Monthly status summaries
Data request log
Field visit photos and notes
Measured Outcomes
1. Accurate drainage subbasins are establishedThe City will have a correct, updated hydrologic picture of the neighborhood.
2. Two fully developed alternatives are ready for comparisonThe City can evaluate feasibility, cost, and constructability.
3. Planning‑level cost estimates are completeThe City can begin budgeting for capital improvements.
4. Permitting pathway is clearly definedThe City will know what permits are required and what hurdles exist.
5. A final Technical Memorandum is deliveredThis becomes the official basis for moving into design and construction.
6. Improved communication with residentsThe graphics and summaries make it easier to explain what the City can realistically do.
title: Resolution 2026-33, A Resolution of the City Commission of the City of Flagler Beach, Florida, approving the proposal from Freese and Nichols, Inc. for the Palm Harbor Drainage Improvements Feasibility Study; authorizing the City Manager to execute the Task Order under the Continuing Services Agreement; providing for findings, for funding, and for an effective date.

description:
DC Blox is developing a new data center facility in the City of Palm Coast, which requires a dedicated electrical grounding and protection system. A portion of the supporting electrical infrastructure for this project traverses the City of Flagler Beach, necessitating the installation of six (6) grounding beds within Flagler Beach’s jurisdiction.
In 2024, the City Commission adopted Resolutions related to the proposed undersea cable landing to support the Palm Coast data center: Resolution 2024-38 determined the fee associated with the necessary easements and Resolution 2024-24 formalized the easement agreement. The easements are in the vicinity of S. 6th Street at S. Oceanshore Boulevard (SR A1A) to serve as the landing site for the undersea cable. The infrastructure associated with the landing site will be constructed within the S. 6th Street right-of-way.
These grounding beds are integral to the safe and compliant operation of the electrical system that will ultimately serve the Palm Coast data center. The grounding beds provide controlled dissipation of fault currents, voltage stabilization, and protection of both equipment and personnel. All installations must comply with the National Electrical Code (NEC), utility standards, and the engineered design submitted to the City.
City staff has reviewed the engineering plans and confirmed:
The six grounding beds are located within approved utility corridors or easements in Flagler Beach.
The installations do not conflict with City utilities, stormwater assets, or planned capital improvements.
The work will be performed by DC Blox’s contractor, with all testing and certification submitted to the City for recordkeeping.
The grounding beds are required to complete the regional electrical interconnection that supports the Palm Coast data center and must be installed to maintain the project’s construction schedule.
The proposed resolution will be considered CONDITIONAL pending State of Florida Communities Trust review and approval.

description:
The City of Flagler Beach maintains an interconnected stormwater swale system throughout the Venice Park neighborhood. These swales serve as the primary means of conveying stormwater runoff during routine rainfall events and play a critical role in reducing roadway ponding, protecting private property, and maintaining overall system performance. Over time, several segments of the swales along Palmetto Avenue, Avalon Avenue, Lantana Avenue, and Lehigh Avenue have experienced sediment buildup, vegetation encroachment, and grade loss, resulting in diminished flow capacity and reduced drainage efficiency.
City staff conducted field evaluations and confirmed that approximately 3,000 linear feet of swales require re‑grading to restore proper slope and conveyance. S.E. Cline Construction, Inc. submitted a written proposal to perform this work, including mobilization, labor, equipment, and maintenance of traffic.
During the assessment, staff also identified that the existing paver driveway at 124 Palmetto Avenue was installed in a manner that obstructs the intended swale flow path, preventing stormwater from moving freely along the roadside drainage system. To correct this condition and restore proper conveyance, Staff proposes to remove the existing pavers and install a new 6‑inch concrete driveway extending up from the Right-Of-Way and includes installation of a 6‑inch trench drain, allowing stormwater to pass beneath the driveway crossing without interruption.

description:
On June 23, 2025, Ms. Midori Imhoof, 261 Ocean Palm Drive, Flagler Beach, Florida, submitted a complaint with the State of Florida Commission on Ethics, "regarding the unethical conduct and neglect the citizens to inform by Mr. Dale Martin in relation to Mr. Jeff Ryan, the leaseholder of the public golf course of Flagler Beach." The documents related to the complaint, the investigation, and the resolution of the complaint are attached, most notably the Final Public Report:
Based on the preliminary investigation of the complaint and the recommendation of the Commission's Advocate, the Commission on Ethics finds there is no probably cause to believe the Respondent, who serves as the City Manager for the City of Flagler Beach, violated Section 112.313(6), Florida Statutes, by corruptly using his official position and/or a resource within his trust to secure a special privilege, benefit, or exemption for himself and/or another; and finds there is no probable cause to believe the Respondent violated Section 112.313(8), Florida Statutes, by using and/or disclosing information not available to the public, and gained by reason of his official position, for the benefit of himself or another, as alleged in the complaint.
Accordingly, this complaint is dismissed with the issuance of this public report.
Ordered by the State of Florida Commission on Ethics meeting in executive session on January 23, 2026.
The City Manager's contract is also attached. Paragraph 17 of the contract states:
17. Indemnification. Employer shall defend, save harmless and indemnify Employee against any tort, professional liability claim or demand or other legal action, whether groundless or otherwise, arising out of an alleged act or omission occurring in the course and scope of Employee' s duties as City Manager or resulting from the exercise of judgment or discretion in connection with the performance of program duties or responsibilities, unless the act or omission involved willful or wanton conduct. Employer may choose, in its sole discretion, the appropriate attorney or firm to represent Employee as provided herein.
Legal representation, provided by Employer for Employee, shall extend until a final determination of the legal action including any appeals brought by either party. Employer shall indemnify Employee against any and all losses, damages, judgments, interest, settlements, fines, court costs and other reasonable costs and expenses of legal proceedings including attorneys fees, and any other liabilities incurred by, imposed upon, or suffered by such Employee in connection with or resulting from any claim, action, suit, or proceeding, actual or threatened, arising out of or in connection with the performance of his or her duties. Any settlement of any claim must be made with prior approval of Employer in order for indemnification, as provided in this Section, to be available.
Employee recognizes that Employer shall have the right to compromise and settle any claim or suit covered by this indemnity obligation. If Employee is a named party to any such litigation or claim, he shall have the right to decline to settle the litigation or claim as to himself, but in such event Employer shall have the right to opt to no longer defend and/ or indemnify Employee.
The City Manager seeks reimbursement for legal and other costs associated with responding to the State of Florida Commission on Ethics Complaint 25-152, totaling $10,783.46 (see attached documentation).

Placement of 3,000 PSI fiber‑reinforced concrete
Broom finish and installation of expansion cuts
Asphalt patching at all disturbed pavement edges
Re‑sodding with Bahia grass for site restoration
Maintenance‑of‑traffic using FDOT‑compliant signage and cones throughout construction

description:
At the March 12, 2026 City Commission Regular Meeting, the City Commission considered a site plan for 1708 S. Oceanshore Blvd. The proposed site plan for a vacation rental facility was subsequently tabled by the City Commission with direction to return the site plan to the Planning and Architectural Review Board for revision and review.
A critical element in the City Commission's decision to table the proposed site plan was the anticipated increased intensity of vehicular traffic in the right-of-way between S. Oceanshore Blvd and S. Central Ave (commonly referred to as an "alley"). Additionally, related to alleys were comments provided during the Public Comment portion of the same meeting regarding the condition of other alleys in the City.
In order to improve the trafficability and sustainability of certain alleys in the City, staff has developed a proposed Standard Design Template for alleys (hereafter designated as "30-foot rights-of-way"). The proposed template makes use of a gridded pattern of heavy-duty pavers (geocells), similar to the pavers used throughout downtown to denote on-street parking areas. The enhanced pavers would be placed upon a substantial base and covered with suitable material, minimizing the visibility of the geocell grid. The intent of City staff is to implement the newly recommended template on 30-foot rights-of-way which provide the sole access to residential properties, specifically portions of Oak Place north of S. 19th St. and the portion of Oak Place south of S. 21st St. If successfully implemented, the additional portion of Oak Place between S. 19th St. and S. 20th St. and Oak Drive could be considered future projects for the use of the proposed Standard Design Template.
title: Resolution 2026-30. A Resolution by the City Commission of the City of Flagler Beach approving the Standard Design Template for 30-foot rights-of-ways; providing for an effective date and providing for conflict.

description:
The City's FY 2025/2026 Annual Budget includes an appropriation ($100,000) for the purchase of a "bucket truck" or lift vehicle. This equipment is intended to provide support for tasks requiring elevated efforts: streetlight maintenance, banner installation, tree trimming, building maintenance, and holiday decorations. At the January 8 City Commission Regular Meeting, the City Commission requested additional information related to the use of such equipment which has previously been rented on an as-needed basis.
During 2025, a lift vehicle was rented for one month (December) for $2,000. The vehicle was utilized for holiday decorations in Veterans Park and elsewhere throughout the City. The vehicle was also utilized to trim palm trees in Veterans Park and Wickline Park, saving the City approximately $11,000 which had previously been expended for professional tree trimming services.
Staff analysis indicates an estimated rental of a lift approximately four times per year to support routine operational needs. While this rental approach has been functional, it presents a significant limitation: the equipment is not guaranteed to be available during urgent or emergency situations. This lack of immediate access introduces operational risk and can delay critical response efforts.
By investing in a City-owned lift, consistent availability, improved readiness, and greater control over scheduling are enhanced. Ownership additionally improves the ability to respond rapidly to unforeseen circumstances, reduces dependency on external vendors, and may yield long-term cost efficiencies. Overall, securing a City lift provides stronger operational resilience and more reliable support for both planned and unplanned tasks.
Although a similar piece of equipment was underutilized and subsequently sold, City staff believes that with the additional staffing funded in the FY 2025/2026, more use could be made of this equipment if re-acquired.
City staff solicited three written quotations for the purchase of a towed boom lift:Everglades Equipment Group: $35,700
Southern States Toyotalift: $39,550
Zuma Sales LLC: $42,485.01
The City Commission requested additional information regarding self-propelled lift equipment and the following pricing information is offered:JLG E519 Telehandler
The E519 represents the mid‑sized option within JLG’s telehandler lineup and is engineered to support a wide range of material handling tasks. With a 5,500‑lb lift capacity and an 18 ft 7 in maximum reach, this unit provides the strength and versatility needed for construction, utility, and facility maintenance operations. Its size and maneuverability make it well suited for confined or developed sites where larger equipment may be impractical. The purchase price for this model is $76,750.00.
JLG H340AJ Articulating Boom Lift
The H340AJ is a self‑propelled articulating boom lift designed to provide safe, efficient elevated access in areas that require up-and-over reach. It offers a 500‑lb platform capacity and a 19 ft 11 in working height, enabling crews to perform maintenance, inspection, and installation tasks with improved precision and mobility. The articulating design enhances access around obstacles, while the self‑propelled chassis supports rapid repositioning on active job sites. The unit is priced at $87,750.00.
City staff believes that the towed boom lift will provide ample support for staff efforts. The equipment is smaller (easier to maneuver in restrictive environments, easier to store when not in use) and easier to transport for use on the west side of the river (not requiring a trailer). Finally, no additional certification/licenses are needed for operators of the towed boom lift. The proposed cost of approximately $30,000 could be recouped in roughly two years, foregoing the need to rent similar equipment and hire additional contractors.
title: Resolution 2026-01. A Resolution by the City Commission of the City of Flagler Beach to accept the lowest responsible quote solicited by the Facilities Department and authorize the purchase of one (1) JLG ET350 Tow-Pro Series Boom Lift from Southern States Toyotalift, in the amount of $35,700.00; providing for conflict and an effective date.

description:
The City of Flagler Beach continues to prioritize stormwater system improvements that reduce localized flooding and enhance community resilience. Swale rehabilitation and maintenance have been identified as critical mitigation needs, particularly in areas where aging or undersized drainage features contribute to stormwater pooling and reduced conveyance capacity.
City staff have obtained competitive quotes for swale maintenance and rehabilitation services for two subdivisions: Venice Park and Palm Circle. These quotes provide a defensible basis for developing the project scope and cost estimate required for the Florida Hurricane Loss Mitigation Program (HLMP). The HLMP provides funding for local mitigation projects that reduce storm‑related vulnerabilities and improve drainage performance.
As required by the State of Florida, all HLMP project applications must be consistent with the Flagler County Local Mitigation Strategy (LMS). The proposed swale rehabilitation project will be submitted to the LMS Working Group for review, prioritization, and inclusion on the approved LMS Project List.
Approval of this resolution authorizes staff to prepare and submit the HLMP application, incorporate the existing quotes into the project proposal, and complete all required LMS coordination.

description:

Mead & Hunt, Inc., under the City’s Continuing Engineering Consulting Services Agreement, submitted a detailed Scope of Services and Fee Proposal dated January 16, 2026, to perform design, permitting, and limited funding assistance for reclaimed water main improvements along Roberts Road and John Anderson Highway. City staff reviewed the proposal and determined that the scope, schedule, and fee are appropriate, consistent with the City’s continuing services contract, and necessary to advance the project toward construction and grant eligibility.

description:
The City of Flagler Beach holds Consumptive Use Permit (CUP) No. 59‑5, issued by the St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD) in October, 2016. The permit authorizes a maximum allocation of 0.912 million gallons per day (MGD) average annual daily demand from the Upper Floridan aquifer and remains in effect until October 11, 2036.
Since the CUP was issued, population growth and updated potable water demand projections indicate that the City’s future water needs will exceed the current allocation. The 2025–2035 Water Supply Facilities Work Plan projects a 2026 population of 7,048 and anticipates potable water demand reaching approximately 2.2 MGD by 2045, an increase of 1.288 MGD above the current allocation.
To support a future CUP modification and renewal, the City must complete groundwater modeling and an impact analysis to evaluate potential effects of increased groundwater withdrawals on wetlands, springs, lakes, rivers, and Minimum Flows and Levels (MFLs). These analyses are required by SJRWMD to determine the viability of increasing the City’s permitted groundwater allocation.
Connect Consulting, Inc. (CCI) submitted a proposal dated February 11, 2026, to perform the following:
Review and update the City’s data within the North Florida–Southeast Georgia (NFSEG) groundwater model.
Conduct groundwater modeling scenarios evaluating impacts of increased withdrawals.
Coordinate with City staff, Mead & Hunt, and SJRWMD, including participation in a pre‑application meeting.
Prepare a signed and sealed Impact Analysis Report.
Provide contingency support for one Request for Additional Information (RAI) from SJRWMD.
CCI proposes to complete this work for a lump‑sum, not‑to‑exceed fee of $48,500.00.
Completion of this modeling effort is necessary to support the City’s long‑term potable water planning and to ensure compliance with regulatory requirements for CUP modification.
title: Resolution 2026-15. A Resolution by the City Commission of the City of Flagler Beach accepting the proposal from Connect Consulting, Inc. for groundwater modeling and impact analysis services in support of the City’s Consumptive Use Permit (CUP) modification and renewal; providing for conflict and an effective date.

description:
The City of Flagler Beach owns and operates a publicly owned treatment works (POTW) that collects and treats wastewater from residential, commercial, and industrial sources. Accumulation of fats, oils, and grease (FOG) within the wastewater collection system has contributed to sewer blockages, system overflows, and increased maintenance costs.
To address these issues, staff has prepared Ordinance 2026-01, which establishes a comprehensive FOG Management Program. The program requires food service establishments to install, maintain, and regularly clean grease interceptors or oil/water separators. It also sets forth inspection protocols, recordkeeping requirements, and enforcement mechanisms to ensure compliance.
This ordinance is intended to protect the City’s wastewater infrastructure, improve system reliability, and comply with state and federal environmental requirements.

description:
Annually, the East Flagler Mosquito Control District is required to obtain authorization for low-level aerial application for control of mosquitoes. This request is required for compliance with Federal Aviation Administration Regulation 137.51, authorization to fly over congested areas.
The East Flagler Mosquito Control District may apply control products by helicopter over or adjacent to congested areas of Flagler County and its municipalities. The purpose of these flights is for surveillance of mosquito breeding sites and the suppression of mosquito populations. Should the need arise, we may also contract with Clarke and Dynamic Aviation, Inc. and Ag Air Services for the same purposes. Flights will normally be performed at an altitude of 500 feet or below.Control of mosquitoes by helicopter is a common practice in populated areas of Florida. The District has conducted aerial mosquito control operations since 1990. All flights will be in the public interest and maximize public safety and mosquito control effectiveness. All control products are approved for control purposes by the Florida Department of Agriculture and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.
For additional information, visit the District website at flaglermosquito.gov, following them on Facebook, or by calling 386-437-0002. The website will map areas to be sprayed by truck or by air and notifications are posted on their Facebook page.

description:
The City of Flagler Beach owns and maintains a stormwater pond located on South Flagler Avenue between South 12th Street and South 13th Street. This pond and its adjoining 220‑foot canal segment play an important role in local drainage, stormwater flow, and water quality management.
On September 12, City Staff reached out to St. John's Water River Water Management District (SJRWMD) for information about removing black mangroves, an endangered species of plant. SJRWMD staff determined that this system (pond adjacent to S. Falgler Ave between S. 12th Str and S. 13th Str) is exempt from permitting pursuant to 62.340 F.A.C. and therefore, pursuant to 403.9328 (5) F.A.C., a permit is not required to trim or alter the mangroves.
City staff have identified the need for restoration activities to improve flow conditions, remove accumulated vegetation, and address obstructions that limit the pond’s performance. Tigris Aquatic Services LLC submitted Quote No. 313721, dated September 23, 2025, proposing a one‑time aquatic restoration project that includes:
Removal of the existing weir structure, riprap, and vegetation in Area 1
Dredging of Area 1 as necessary to achieve adequate flow
Clearing vegetation back three feet on both sides of the 220‑foot canal
Cleaning the canal to improve flow
Removal of Lyngbya from the pond surface and banks
Re-Install the Weir Structure after cleaning
All labor, materials, equipment, and remediation necessary to complete the project
Staff have reviewed the proposal and determined that the scope of work is appropriate and necessary to support stormwater system performance in this area.
title: Resolution 2026-06. A Resolution by the City Commission of the City of Flagler Beach accepting Quote No. 313721 from Tigris Aquatic Services LLC for aquatic restoration work at the stormwater pond located on South Flagler Avenue between South 12th Street and South 13th Street, in an amount not to exceed $34,235.00; providing for conflict and an effective date.

Flagler Beach Fire Department Fire Station Renovation

description:
The existing training room at Fire Station 11 no longer meets the operational, administrative, or personnel support needs of a modern fire station. Currently configured as a single, underutilized space, the room does not efficiently support operational readiness, daily coordination, or the well-being of on-duty personnel. After evaluating station needs and workflow, staff determined that reconfiguring the space into two clearly defined functional areas, a dedicated day room and a dedicated administrative/operational workspace, will substantially improve efficiency, productivity, and quality of life for personnel.
This renovation represents a strategic investment in both operational effectiveness and employee welfare.
The renovation will:
Establish a stand-alone day room by relocating recliners from the kitchen/dining area, eliminating the overlap between meal preparation, dining, and rest activities and restoring appropriate separation of functions.
Create a dedicated administrative workspace that supports planning, training coordination, reporting, interagency collaboration, and daily operational management for multiple organizations.
Improve lighting quality and reduce long-term utility costs through installation of energy-efficient LED fixtures.
Strengthen technology readiness with structured network cabling to support computers, printers, and telephone systems.
Replace worn flooring and baseboard trim to improve durability, safety, and overall workplace comfort.
Lads Coastal Construction LLC submitted Proposal 6‑17, dated January 26, 2026, outlining the renovation scope, bid alternates, and a 10% contingency allowance. The total proposed cost is $42,967.21.
Staff have reviewed the proposal and recommends approval, noting that the renovation represents a cost‑effective use of existing space and aligns with modern fire station design standards.
The recommended contractor was selected based on their existing Continuing Services Contract with the City of Flagler Beach, awarded through RFQ 25‑1806. Utilizing a firm already procured through a competitive, qualifications‑based process ensures full compliance with City and State procurement requirements and enables the project to advance without delay.
The contractor has an established record of successful performance for the City, including completion of the City Hall renovations, improvements at the Flagler Beach Library, and work for the Police Department. Their familiarity with City facilities, operational standards, and expectations provides added value and reduces project risk.
City staff engaged in multiple rounds of scope refinement and cost negotiations with the contractor to align the work elements with the approved project budget. The final negotiated amount represents a fair and reasonable price consistent with the rates and terms of the continuing contract.
Approval of this renovation will enhance operational readiness, improve working conditions for personnel, and ensure the space functions in a manner consistent with the demands placed on today’s fire service professionals.

description:
Short-term rental properties have become an increasingly common form of lodging within the City of Flagler Beach, accommodating residents, visitors, and seasonal guests. Unlike traditional owner-occupied dwellings, short-term rentals experience frequent occupant turnover, varying levels of familiarity with the property, and increased use of cooking, heating, and electrical systems. These factors elevate the potential risk for fire incidents and life-safety emergencies.
Fire inspections of short-term rental properties are conducted to ensure compliance with applicable fire codes, life-safety standards, and local ordinances. The primary objective of these inspections is to reduce the risk of fire, ensure early detection and warning, provide safe means of egress, and protect occupants, neighboring properties, and responding emergency personnel.
By implementing a standardized inspection process for short-term rentals, the Flagler Beach Fire Department promotes a consistent level of safety. This program supports community risk reduction efforts, enhances public safety, and ensures that property owners meet their responsibility to provide a safe environment for occupants while operating a short-term rental within the jurisdiction.

description:
On January 24, a 45-foot sailboat was grounded offshore in the vicinity of N. 21st Street and N. Oceanshore Blvd (SR A1A). Fire Department personnel successfully rescued the occupants and the vessel subsequently washed ashore in that same area. A smaller motorboat (associated with the sailboat) also washed ashore. Although the motorboat was successfully removed from the beach (Jan 29), the sailboat remains. The vessel was noticed in accordance with State statutes on Jan 29, providing that the owner has twenty-one days to remove the vessel. If the vessel is not removed by Feb 20, the City can remove the sailboat.
Acting Police Chief Blanchette has provided the following background information related to the beaching of the sailboat:
The owner is trying to relinquish ownership of this vessel, possibly to avoid responsibility and fees, which I DO NOT recommend we do. If we take ownership, we forego the possibility of recovering any removal expenses from the owner (civil) and potential criminal charges for the derelict vessel. We would also no longer be able to recover monies through any available grants.
A certified letter was mailed (and hand-delivered) to the vessel’s registered owner. Under state statute, this would constitute official notification.
The removal of the boat will cost the City approximately $50,000.00 to $75,000.00 up front, which may be partially reimbursed by a state grant or St. Johns Waterway. We would also have the option to seek reimbursement from the owner, as their insurance specifically does not cover recovery costs.
The other option is to allow the Florida Wildlife Commission to handle the derelict boat; this will take an estimated eight months to complete. This creates a significant safety hazard, as within that timeline, the vessel may break up, increasing risk. While the vessel has been pumped dry of fuel, it does still contain a high volume of oil.
The Police Department has completed two separate reports on these vessels (They are being treated as two separate derelict vessels). The case numbers are 2026-00001296 (Sailboat at 21st St. N) and 2026-00001298 (Jet Boat at 12th Street N)
To expedite the removal process, the City Commission is asked to consider an intergovernmental procurement agreement based upon the efforts of St. Augustine. St. Augustine has extensive experience in the removal of derelict boats and has provided Acting Police Chief Blanchette significant insights on how to proceed with the removal. If the proposed Resolution is approved, City staff will begin coordination with one of the authorized salvage companies to have the vessel removed on Feb 20.
title: Resolution 2026-11. description:
Short-term rental properties have become an increasingly common form of lodging within the City of Flagler Beach, accommodating residents, visitors, and seasonal guests. Unlike traditional owner-occupied dwellings, short-term rentals experience frequent occupant turnover, varying levels of familiarity with the property, and increased use of cooking, heating, and electrical systems. These factors elevate the potential risk for fire incidents and life-safety emergencies.
Fire inspections of short-term rental properties are conducted to ensure compliance with applicable fire codes, life-safety standards, and local ordinances. The primary objective of these inspections is to reduce the risk of fire, ensure early detection and warning, provide safe means of egress, and protect occupants, neighboring properties, and responding emergency personnel.
By implementing a standardized inspection process for short-term rentals, the Flagler Beach Fire Department promotes a consistent level of safety. This program supports community risk reduction efforts, enhances public safety, and ensures that property owners meet their responsibility to provide a safe environment for occupants while operating a short-term rental within the jurisdiction.

description:
A Fire Department Command Vehicle plays a critical role in incident command, emergency response coordination, and special events requiring unified command and communications. One of the current vehicles has reached the end of its service life due to impacts of a hurricane, resulting in increased maintenance needs, reduced reliability, and safety concerns. The proposed action is a one-for-one replacement as part of the City’s scheduled fleet replacement program. Replacing the vehicle at this stage is more cost-effective than continued maintenance and reduces the risk of operational downtime as well as accidents/injury. The replacement vehicle will be properly equipped to support incident command functions and will not expand the City’s fleet.
Funding for this replacement has been anticipated through the city’s capital replacement process. Approval will ensure continued reliability, operational readiness, and responsible stewardship of City assets in support of public safety operations.

description:
The City of Flagler Beach has initiated the Wastewater Treatment Plant Biological Nutrient Removal (BNR) Improvements Project to modernize its wastewater treatment facilities, reduce nutrient discharges, and comply with evolving state environmental regulations, including Florida Senate Bill 64 (2021).
To ensure successful implementation and quality assurance during construction, the City advertised a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) and Proposal solicitation for Professional Construction Engineering and Inspection (CEI) Services under Bid No. FB-25-0414.
The City received only one proposal. City staff reviewed the proposal and upon evaluation, McKim & Creed, Inc. was determined to be the most qualified and responsive firm to provide CEI services for this critical project.
McKim & Creed’s proposal, dated May 28, 2025, includes a comprehensive scope of services covering project management, on-site construction observation, engineering office support, and monitoring of funding requirements. The project’s estimated construction duration is approximately 23 months (700 days).

description:
Chapter 2025-182, Laws of Florida, which was formerly known as Senate Bill 954, establishes new regulatory requirements for certified recovery residences in Florida, effective July 1, 2025. Pursuant to Section 397.487, Florida Statutes, "By January 1, 2026, the governing body of each county or municipality shall adopt an ordinance establishing procedures for the review and approval of certified recovery residences within its jurisdiction. The ordinance must include a process for requesting reasonable accommodations from any local land use regulation that serves to prohibit the establishment of a certified recovery residence." These facilities, commonly known as sober homes, offer structured, supportive living environments for individuals recovering from substance-use disorders. Typically operated as group living arrangements, recovery residences can present zoning and land use challenges related to occupancy limits, neighborhood compatibility, and use classifications. In the 2025 legislative session, the Florida Legislature passed Senate Bill 954, which requires local governments to adopt an ordinance to establish a process for applicants seeking reasonable accommodations from land use regulations that serve to prohibit the establishment of a certified recovery residence. On June 25, 2025, Governor DeSantis approved Senate Bill 954, and Senate Bill 954 was codified into law as Chapter 2025-182. The proposed LDC amendment complies with the statutory requirements of Section 397.487, Florida Statutes.
An applicant shall not be entitled to a reasonable accommodation if the requested accommodation is incompatible with surrounding uses and structures in the zoning district, is not substantially similar to surrounding uses and structures expressly permitted in the zoning district, and the city has not otherwise routinely waived the applicable ordinance, rule, policy, practice or procedure. A requested increase in density shall not be considered reasonable accommodation. The applicant shall demonstrate that the proposed accommodation does not impose an undue financial or administrative burden on the city.
title: Ordinance 2025-29. An Ordinance of the City of Flagler Beach, Florida, relating to the Land Development Regulations; amending the Code of Ordinances to add Section 8.06.01 to Appendix “A,” “Land Development Regulations,” establishing a process for the review of reasonable accommodation requests for certified recovery residences pursuant to Florida Statutes Section 397.487; providing for conflicts; providing for codification; providing for severability; and providing an effective date - (Second [Final] Reading).

description:
The City of Flagler Beach operates a potable water distribution system that provides essential service to residents and businesses. To ensure reliability and reduce costly maintenance, the City is replacing aging infrastructure through the South Central Water Main Replacement Project.
Phase 1 of the project was recently completed, replacing older water mains between Moody Boulevard and 3rd Street. This work improved water flow, reduced leaks, and modernized a critical section of the system. Mead & Hunt served as the design consultant for Phase 1, providing construction oversight and technical support.
Phase 2 will extend these improvements southward along South Central Avenue, from 3rd Street to 6th Street. Work includes:
Installing new water mains and service connections,
Replacing valves and related fittings,

description:
The City of Flagler Beach entered into a contract with Vecellio & Grogan, Inc. (V&G) for the Flagler Beach Fishing Pier Removal and Replacement Project (Contract No. 260). During construction, several unforeseen and unavoidable conditions occurred, resulting in schedule impacts and additional costs outside the control of the contractor.
Following review by the City Engineer and the City’s Construction Engineering and Inspection Advisor, England-Thims & Miller, Inc. (ETM), the delays and associated costs were confirmed as valid and appropriate for an equitable adjustment under the contract. These issues include:
FDEP Permit Restrictions – Marine Turtle Nest #1
A marine turtle nest was identified on July 2, 2025, within 20 feet of the planned trestle alignment. Pursuant to FDEP Permit Modification No. 0436370-002-JN, construction was prohibited within this buffer zone. To maintain compliance and avoid suspension of critical-path work, the trestle had to be redesigned and modified, requiring additional engineering and non-standard components.
Compensation: $1,275.90
Additional Days: 0
Unmarked Electrical Line Strike
On July 23, 2025, V&G struck an unmarked, City-owned electrical line that was not shown in utility records and not identified through Sunshine 811 locates. This resulted in an immediate work stoppage and required coordination with FPL to safely de-energize the line. The resulting standby time, equipment demobilization, and utility exposure costs are compensable under the contract.
Compensation: $10,938.32
Additional Days: 0
FDEP Permit Restrictions – Marine Turtle Nest #2
A second active turtle nest was located on July 27, 2025, directly within the trestle footprint, requiring a full suspension of trestle installation for an estimated 50–70 days until hatching occurred. No feasible alternative construction methods existed that would maintain compliance with FDEP and wildlife regulations.
Compensation: $94,784.07
Additional Days: 36
Builder’s Risk Insurance Premium Adjustment
The builder’s risk policy premium required adjustment from the original estimate after final underwriting, which incorporated surplus lines taxes, broker fees, administrative costs, and confirmation of total project value. These elements could not be fully determined during bidding.
Compensation: $37,203.38
Additional Days: 0
Inclement Weather and Holiday Days
A review of daily reports from August 1 through October 28, 2025, validated four (4) non-working days: three (3) due to inclement weather and one (1) contractual holiday. These qualify as excusable, non-compensable delays.
Compensation: $0.00
Additional Days: 4
Requested Adjustment (Change Order No. 02)
The combined impact of the events above results in:
Total Cost Adjustment: $144,201.67
Total Time Adjustment: 40 days
Approval of Change Order No. 02 will revise the substantial completion date to January 15, 2027, and the final completion date to February 14, 2027.

description:
OverviewIn past sessions, the Florida Legislature amended Section 934.50, Florida Statutes to require governmental entities to only utilize drones meeting the requirements outlined in Rule 60GG-2.0075, Florida Administrative Code. This change required governmental agencies who use drones for various purposes to cease the use of any drone that is not in compliance with the Rule.
During the 2023 Legislative Session, the Florida Department of Law Enforcement appropriated approximately $25 million in nonrecurring funds to implement the Drone Replacement Grant Program. This grant provides funding for the Recipient to acquire drones that are in compliance with Rule 60GG-2.0075, Florida Administrative Code.EligibilityFrom July 15, 2025, through October 14, 2025, FDLE will be accepting applications from:
• law enforcement agencies (LEAs), fire service providers, ambulance crews, or other first responders defined in statute who have NOT received any funding under this program since its inception in FY23-24
• law enforcement agencies (LEAs), fire service providers, ambulance crews, or other first responders defined in statute who are located in Florida’s fiscally constrained counties, even if previous funding was received
Pending remaining available funding, FDLE will open the solicitation on October 15, 2025, to all law enforcement agencies (LEAs), fire service providers, ambulance crews, or other first responders defined in statute, including those who received funding in prior years. What We Were AwardedOfficer Jones applied for this grant as the City of Flagler Beach and requested funding for 4 drones at $25,000 each. They awarded us all 4 drones and approved $100,000 towards the purchase of those drones. Attached is the vendor quote for the drones and this will be submitted to FDLE with the cash advance option form.
Payment OptionsThere are two options to receive the award:
1. Cash Advance option where FDLE will provide funds in advance for the purchase of pre-approved drones (this is the option chosen for the city). This option requires submission of a vendor quote, plus a valid Purchase Order for the drones. The agreement states: “The recipient may request a cash advance to receive program funds and subsequently purchase the compliant drone(s). In order to qualify for this method of payment, the recipient must provide a valid, executed purchase order and must be ready to order the compliant drone(s) immediately upon the receipt of advanced funds. The recipient must provide documentation of purchase (invoice) and proof of payment (canceled check, bank/card statement, etc.) within 45 days of receiving the advanced funds. Failure to provide documentation within 45 days will result in the recipient being required to submit a refund to FDLE.”
2. Reimbursement of funds: This option allows FDLE to reimburse the city for the funds after they have been purchased. The agreement states: “The recipient may use its own funds to purchase the compliant drone(s) and provide documentation related to the purchase including: purchase order, invoice, and proof of payment (canceled check, bank/card statement, etc.).”
https://www.fdle.state.fl.us/fdle-grants/open-funding-opportunities/drone/fy24-25-drone-1
Equipment the City will be receivingWe currently use a Skydio X2E drone. Skydio is one of the companies the US Government has approved for military and government agencies to utilize for drones. This was to eliminate any information or data being sent to China through other drone manufacturers. From Axon Enterprises, Inc, as a sole source vendor, we have requested the Skydio X10 for our new drone, which is an excellent upgrade from the X2E. It flies faster, has better cameras, better collision avoidance, fleet management capability, external speaker, Axon video upload, and in March 2026, they should be releasing a payload drop option for purchase.
The first drone we had came with a speaker so we could fly the drone out to boats on the water who were called in as being in distress and verify if they needed Coast Guard assistance. Using a speaker also allows us to give commands to a suspect or subject if needed. Our first drone also had the capability to drop a life preserver to a swimmer in need of rescue due to riptides, exhaustion, or other medical emergencies. However, our first drone was made by a company that is no longer authorized for government use. Then we purchased the Skydio X2E but it did not have the speaker or payload capability. Now with the X10, we will have a speaker and next year they should be releasing the payload capability as an add-on. This will allow us to utilize the drone for enhanced rescue support.
Here is where more information is available about the Skydio X10: https://www.skydio.com/x10

description:
Chapter 2025-182, Laws of Florida, which was formerly known as Senate Bill 954, establishes new regulatory requirements for certified recovery residences in Florida, effective July 1, 2025. Pursuant to Section 397.487, Florida Statutes, "By January 1, 2026, the governing body of each county or municipality shall adopt an ordinance establishing procedures for the review and approval of certified recovery residences within its jurisdiction. The ordinance must include a process for requesting reasonable accommodations from any local land use regulation that serves to prohibit the establishment of a certified recovery residence." These facilities, commonly known as sober homes, offer structured, supportive living environments for individuals recovering from substance-use disorders. Typically operated as group living arrangements, recovery residences can present zoning and land use challenges related to occupancy limits, neighborhood compatibility, and use classifications. In the 2025 legislative session, the Florida Legislature passed Senate Bill 954, which requires local governments to adopt an ordinance to establish a process for applicants seeking reasonable accommodations from land use regulations that serve to prohibit the establishment of a certified recovery residence. On June 25, 2025, Governor DeSantis approved Senate Bill 954, and Senate Bill 954 was codified into law as Chapter 2025-182. The proposed LDC amendment complies with the statutory requirements of Section 397.487, Florida Statutes.
An applicant shall not be entitled to a reasonable accommodation if the requested accommodation is incompatible with surrounding uses and structures in the zoning district, is not substantially similar to surrounding uses and structures expressly permitted in the zoning district, and the city has not otherwise routinely waived the applicable ordinance, rule, policy, practice or procedure. A requested increase in density shall not be considered reasonable accommodation. The applicant shall demonstrate that the proposed accommodation does not impose an undue financial or administrative burden on the city.
title: Ordinance 2025- 29. An Ordinance of the City of Flagler Beach, Florida, relating to the Land Development Regulations; amending the Code of Ordinances to add Section 8.06.01 to Appendix “A,” “Land Development Regulations,” establishing a process for the review of reasonable accommodation requests for certified recovery residences pursuant to Florida Statutes Section 397.487; providing for conflicts; providing for codification; providing for severability; and providing an effective date (First Reading).

description:
The City of Flagler Beach continues to experience growth that is increasing potable water demand while several existing wells are showing reduced water quality and yield. To address these needs, two parcels were previously dedicated to the city as New Well Sites #1 and #2, intended for Wells #17 and #18.
Mead & Hunt, Inc. has prepared a proposal dated October 13, 2025, to provide engineering design and permitting services for these new wells and to assist with the Consumptive Use Permit (CUP) modification required by the St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD). description:
The City of Flagler Beach maintains an extensive network of fire hydrants (nearly 300) vital to community fire protection and public safety. Routine inspections and maintenance conducted by City staff and contracted personnel have identified multiple hydrants requiring immediate repair or replacement due to age, corrosion, and mechanical failure.
To ensure compliance with Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) and National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) standards, prompt corrective action is necessary. The City has an established continuing services contract with U.S. Water Services Corporation, which provides qualified personnel, equipment, and expertise to perform such work efficiently and in accordance with City procurement requirements.

attachments.name: Butterfly Garden Authorization Request from Property Owner Keith Patton

description:
The property and local business owner at 324 N 2nd Street is seeking authorization to place a butterfly garden around a monument sign that will grow to encompass part of the right-of-way.
Per City Code Sec. 14-108 — Regulations governing the placement and maintenance of vegetation and improvements within public right-of-way, public ways, and other public property.
1. The request for authorization includes a statement demonstrating that the placement and maintenance of the vegetation or improvement will not: (1) create visual blight; (2) pose a safety hazard to the traveling public including any impairment of safe lines of sight; (3) diminish or interfere with the function, maintenance, or operation of the public right-of-way, public way or public property including swales and other stormwater retention, detention, and transmission infrastructure; or (4) otherwise harm the health, safety, or welfare of the community wherein the vegetation or improvement is to be located. This section shall not apply to any developer of land required as part of the development approvals to install infrastructure or vegetation within a right-of-way or upon other public property.
The applicant reviewed the butterfly garden concept with City Engineer, Bill Freeman, who confirmed that Section 14-108 (3) will not be affected by the request.
Sec. 5.03.42. — Access to water meters for city meter readers. All owners of real property and/or tenants of real property receiving water from the city water system and having a water meter located on their property or the city's right-of-way abutting their property shall be responsible for keeping the area from the edge of the roadway up to and within a two-foot radius of the water meter free of shrubbery, plant life, automobiles, fences and other materials which might prevent ready and convenient access to the water meter by the city meter reader at all times.
The applicant acknowledged he is to maintain a two-foot radius around the water meter clear of material, shrubbery, and debris.
title: Consider the request from the property owner at 324 N 2nd Street to place a butterfly garden around the monument sign and City ROW.

attachments.name: Well 17 and 18 Scope of Services Revised 2.0

description:
The City of Flagler Beach continues to experience growth that is increasing potable water demand while several existing wells are showing reduced water quality and yield. To address these needs, two parcels were previously dedicated to the city as New Well Sites #1 and #2, intended for Wells #17 and #18.
Mead & Hunt, Inc. has prepared a proposal dated October 13, 2025, to provide engineering design and permitting services for these new wells and to assist with the Consumptive Use Permit (CUP) modification required by the St. Johns River Water Management District (SJRWMD). The proposal also includes coordination with Connect Consulting, Inc. (CCI) for well drilling and groundwater modeling, and Biological Consulting Services, Inc. (BCS) for wetland monitoring plan updates.
This project is critical to maintaining the City’s potable water capacity and ensuring long-term water supply reliability in compliance with regulatory requirements.
title: Resolution 2025-91. description:
The City of Flagler Beach Wastewater Treatment Facility (WWTF) Biological Nutrient Removal (BNR) Improvements Project (FDEP Project No. WW180131) is a major capital improvement effort designed to enhance nutrient removal processes, improve operational efficiency, and ensure compliance with modern state and federal water quality standards.
Bids for construction were solicited and evaluated in accordance with City and Florida Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) State Revolving Fund (SRF) Program requirements. Following the evaluation, L7 Construction Inc. was determined to be the lowest responsive and responsible bidder, with a total bid amount of $46,307,000.
On October 20, 2025, FDEP issued an award authorization letter granting the City approval to proceed with awarding the contract to L7 Construction Inc. The project will be funded through the SRF loan and grant program, with funds disbursed as they become available.
title: Resolution 2025-92. A Resolution by the City Commission of the City of Flagler Beach, Florida, authorizing the award of Contract WW180131 to L7 Construction Inc. for the Flagler Beach Wastewater Treatment Facility (WWTF) Biological Nutrient Removal (BNR) Improvements Project in the amount of $46,307,000; authorizing the contract and related documents; and providing for conflict and an effective date.
